p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.
More reading
How Prop. 3 fared in Berkeley poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax) (L.A. Times)

Inside the Prop. 3 campaign (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043) (EdSource)
Proposition 4
The basics
Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on the public funding of campaigns and allow all local and state governments to offer public financing programs with certain conditions.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 4: Allowing public campaign financing in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide)
Prop 4 would repeal California’s 1988 ban on public campaign financing, allowing state and local governments to create programs for candidates seeking office.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Candidates would have to abide by certain expenditure limits and follow strict criteria. Funds could not be used for legal or defense purposes or to repay personal loans, nor could they be pulled from education, transportation or public safety buckets. The ballot measure also prohibits discrimination based on party or whether a candidate is an incumbent or running in opposition.
Dig deeper
Democrats and many good government groups support it. The California Taxpayers Assn. and Reform California oppose it.
Proposition 5
The basics
Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years. In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). But in 2003, Gray Davis was ousted from office (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html) and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger. Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.
Advertisement
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide)
Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Dig deeper
California’s rules for recalling politicians date to the Progressive era (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html) and were seen at the time as a way to give more power to voters.
But there have been concerns in recent years that the process needs reform, especially after the 2021 recall that Newsom overwhelmingly beat back; it cost local and state governments more than $200 million.
After the Newsom recall failed, the Legislature began a bipartisan task force to suggest changes.
Advertisement
More reading
California’s costly, confusing recall sparks an effort to rethink the rules (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-15/california-costly-confusing-gavin-newsom-recall-rethink-the-rules) (L.A. Times, 2021)
The history of recalls in California (https://www.latimes.com/projects/california-recall-history-insights-from-elections-petitions/) (L.A. Times)
The Little Hoover Commission on recall reform (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) (State of California)
Proposition 37
The basics
California’s Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained) would authorize up to $25 billion in down-payment loans for eligible middle-income buyers.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Prop. 37 offers $25 billion to homebuyers to help with a down payment. Here’s the catch (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained)
California’s Prop. 37 could provide $25 billion for homebuyer down payments. Learn how the middle-class housing measure works and its key caveats.
Oct. 24, 2026
The impact
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds. The program would not be funded by taxpayers but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down-payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building. The proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure was approved.
Dig deeper
The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José. Supporters say restricting the program to new homes could spur construction. But critics warn down-payment debt could burden buyers and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.
Proposition 38
The basics
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year. Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 38: Immunology and immunotherapy research funding (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide)
Prop 38 aims to fund immunotherapy research to prevent and cure diseases through bonds. An opponent says it is a debt-financed model that prioritizes a few diseases.
Oct. 26, 2026
The impact
The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s. It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The Yes on 38 campaign says the proposition pays for itself; 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the state to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. However, it’s difficult to predict whether any research projects will lead to marketable treatments.
Dig deeper
Proposition 38 was backed by organizations including the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research and the ALS Assn. as well as a majority of local chapters of Democratic organizations across the state. Supporters say the proposed funding could give those afflicted with chronic illness hope and potentially more options for treatment.
Its opponents have said the proposed criteria for awarding the grant funding would appear to create an extremely small pool of qualified recipients. Only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, co-founded by billionaire Gary K. Michelson, would qualify under the proposed criteria, according to No on 38.
Advertisement
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for Yes on 38, said “lots of institutions would qualify for funds under this measure.” But she said at a virtual news conference in mid-September that it was “very likely” that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy “will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria.”
Ultimately, Swanson said, the decision lies with the California Department of Public Health.
More reading
An analysis of Prop. 38 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026) (California Legislative Analyst’s Office)
This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) (Cal Matters)
This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) (Cal Matters)
Proposition 39
The basics
Proposition 39 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-39-voting-id-requirements-voter-guide) would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote. In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 39: Stricter voter ID requirements (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-39-voting-id-requirements-voter-guide)
Prop 39 brings the national debate around U.S. election integrity home to California by proposing stricter new voter identification and citizenship verification requirements for state elections.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Opponents contend — as do many independent election experts — that California already has robust measures for verifying the eligibility and identity of voters, and that voter fraud, including by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare. The measure is opposed by the state’s Democratic establishment and prominent civil rights groups, who say it will disenfranchise many eligible voters, particularly those of color, who are poor or live in rural communities. Backers — who include prominent California Republicans and ultrawealthy supporters of President Trump — say it is necessary to prevent voter fraud and block noncitizens from casting ballots. They have provided little evidence of widespread fraud.
Advertisement
Dig deeper
This is part of a larger national campaign. After his return to the White House last year, Trump began a fresh crusade (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing) to rewrite election laws across the country.
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some of California’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they have spent a fortune in an effort to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.
Advertisement
More reading
A powerful union and the birth of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) (L.A. Times)
Why unions are divided over Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-30/labor-organizers-spearheading-california-billionaire-tax-rebuffed-by-parent-union) (L.A. Times)
The Google co-founder fighting the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax) (L.A. Times)
Inside the massive spending to defeat Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) (L.A. Times)
How the billionaire tax could spark national movement (https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/10/12/the-battle-to-pass-a-billionaire-tax) (The New Yorker)
The academics behind Prop. 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) (Sacramento Bee)
Will Prop. 40 really bring an exodus? (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus) (L.A. Times)
Why healthcare is divided by Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/science/story/2026-09-28/billionaire-tax-is-dividing-california-healthcare-system-its-designed-to-support) (Bloomberg)
Taxing the “ultrarich,” a guide (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/13/magazine/billionaire-wealth-tax-proposition-40.html) (New York Times)
Proposition 41
The basics
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Proposition 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Dig deeper
The California Taxpayers Assn., the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and others back the proposition. They say it would result in the government spending taxpayer dollars more wisely while improving transparency.
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group behind the proposed billionaire tax, opposes Proposition 41. In arguments against the measure, SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote that the billionaires don’t care about government accountability and have been avoiding higher taxes through loopholes and tax breaks.
Proposition 42
The basics
Proposition 42 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide) would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
Advertisement
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)

Prop 39 brings the national debate around U.S. election integrity home to California by proposing stricter new voter identification and citizenship verification requirements for state elections.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Opponents contend — as do many independent election experts — that California already has robust measures for verifying the eligibility and identity of voters, and that voter fraud, including by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare. The measure is opposed by the state’s Democratic establishment and prominent civil rights groups, who say it will disenfranchise many eligible voters, particularly those of color, who are poor or live in rural communities. Backers — who include prominent California Republicans and ultrawealthy supporters of President Trump — say it is necessary to prevent voter fraud and block noncitizens from casting ballots. This is part of a larger national campaign. After his return to the White House last year, Trump began a fresh crusade (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing) to rewrite election laws across the country.
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.

Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.

The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.

The basics

Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.

The measure states that its purpose is to protect Californians’ ability to save for retirement and the future, though opponents say it’s meant to trick voters into canceling the billionaire tax.

Oct. 1, 2026

If the proposition passes, the state attorney general will be responsible for determining what services fall into that category

The basics

Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Candidates would have to abide by certain expenditure limits and follow strict criteria. Funds could not be used for legal or defense purposes or to repay personal loans, nor could they be pulled from education, transportation or public safety buckets. The ballot measure also prohibits discrimination based on party or whether a candidate is an incumbent or running in opposition.
Dig deeper
Democrats and many good government groups support it. The California Taxpayers Assn. and Reform California oppose it.

The basics
Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years. In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). But in 2003, Gray Davis was ousted from office (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html) and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger. Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.
Advertisement
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)

Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Dig deeper
California’s rules for recalling politicians date to the Progressive era (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html) and were seen at the time as a way to give more power to voters.
But there have been concerns in recent years that the process needs reform, especially after the 2021 recall that Newsom overwhelmingly beat back; it cost local and state governments more than $200 million.
After the Newsom recall failed, the Legislature began a bipartisan task force to suggest changes.

More reading

Supporters say restricting the program to new homes could spur construction. Prop 38 aims to fund immunotherapy research to prevent and cure diseases through bonds. An opponent says it is a debt-financed model that prioritizes a few diseases.

PPIC's 65% support, including a split Republican vote, looks strong for a $25B bond, which I'd read as a sign the GOP's neutrality is helping. I'm fairly confident in Yes, but I'll still check the Hoover analysis and any late "No on 37" committee.

## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.

# Proposition 37
## Should the state be authorized to issue $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a “middle-class” homebuyer down-payment assistance program?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 would create a down-payment assistance program for families earning up to 200% of an area’s median income — the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area — adjusted for household size.
This assistance could only be used to buy newly constructed homes.
The bond would be repaid through the mortgages of participating homebuyers.
## Yes Argument
For many Californians, the biggest barrier to buying a home is the down payment.
This measure is designed for the “missing middle” — working families who earn too much for most other down-payment assistance programs but still cannot save enough to buy a home.
Proposition 37 reduces the required down payment to just 3%.
## No Argument
Proposition 37 provides taxpayer-funded subsidies to developers without reforming costly mandates that make housing expensive.
Worse, Proposition 37 makes the state of California one of the biggest mortgage lenders in America overnight — and taxpayers are left holding the bag.

This list is not exhaustive, and may be updated.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Yes. Prop 37 will very likely pass. I couldn't find any results yet. The latest pages I found are from November 2, 2026, the day before the election, so this is a forecast and not a result.

- **Polls:** The Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) had it at 65% yes and 32% no in late October, up from 61–35 in September. It was the strongest of the 14 measures on the ballot. A separate AIMSA poll of 2,000 likely voters (October 19–24) found 59% support. PPIC found majorities in favor across regions and demographic groups. Even Republicans were nearly split, 47% yes to 51% no.
- **Money:** The yes side raised about $33–35 million, mostly from the Realtors, the carpenters' unions and Building a Better California. No opposition committee reported any contributions, and no argument against it was filed for the state voter guide.
- **Supporters:** Governor Newsom, Becerra (the Democratic nominee for governor, leading by 24–27 points), the state Democratic Party, the state labor federation, the California Teachers Association, SEIU and the California Chamber of Commerce all back it. The state Republican Party stayed neutral.
- **Opponents:** The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the League of Women Voters, Reform California, a few minor parties and several newspapers oppose it. They ran no paid campaign.
- **Ballot wording:** The ballot summary says "no direct state or local costs," because the homebuyers' loan payments repay the bonds, not taxpayers.

**Caveat:** PPIC has overstated support for bonds before. In the March 2024 primary it had Prop 1 at 59%, and that measure passed with only 50.2%. Even a gap that large would still leave Prop 37 above 50%. In the November 2024 election, PPIC's bond numbers were close to the actual results.

I'm also checking whether the crowded ballot with several bond measures could drag this one down, but the PPIC numbers show even the bonds polling around 57 to 60 percent. The general mood is sour and the Democratic enthusiasm edge is large, which still points toward a yes outcome.

content.text:
Yes. Prop 37 will very likely pass. I couldn't find any results yet. The latest pages I found are from November 2, 2026, the day before the election, so this is a forecast and not a result.

- **Polls:** The Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) had it at 65% yes and 32% no in late October, up from 61–35 in September. It was the strongest of the 14 measures on the ballot. A separate AIMSA poll of 2,000 likely voters (October 19–24) found 59% support. PPIC found majorities in favor across regions and demographic groups. Even Republicans were nearly split, 47% yes to 51% no.
- **Money:** The yes side raised about $33–35 million, mostly from the Realtors, the carpenters' unions and Building a Better California. No opposition committee reported any contributions, and no argument against it was filed for the state voter guide.
- **Supporters:** Governor Newsom, Becerra (the Democratic nominee for governor, leading by 24–27 points), the state Democratic Party, the state labor federation, the California Teachers Association, SEIU and the California Chamber of Commerce all back it. The state Republican Party stayed neutral.
- **Opponents:** The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the League of Women Voters, Reform California, a few minor parties and several newspapers oppose it. They ran no paid campaign.
- **Ballot wording:** The ballot summary says "no direct state or local costs," because the homebuyers' loan payments repay the bonds, not taxpayers.

**Caveat:** PPIC has overstated support for bonds before. In the March 2024 primary it had Prop 1 at 59%, and that measure passed with only 50.2%. Even a gap that large would still leave Prop 37 above 50%. In the November 2024 election, PPIC's bond numbers were close to the actual results.

yes

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Revenue Bonds. Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
PROPOSAL
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middleclass homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.” Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
FISCAL EFFECTS
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.

CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 37
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 37: the California Middle- Class Homeownership & Family Home Construction Act. Proposition 37 creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction-with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
California has the second-worst homeownership rate in the nation; rising costs push homeownership further out of reach every year.
With the statewide median home price now exceeding $930,000, a traditional 20% down payment can require saving over $186,000 just to get in the door. Teachers, nurses, veterans, and firefighters work hard and pay their bills. They can afford monthly mortgage payments but are locked out of homeownership in the communities where they live and work because down payment requirements are too high.
Proposition 37 gives working and middle-class Californians a fair shot at homeownership.
KEEPING HOMEOWNERSHIP WITHIN REACH.
Prop. 37 is a practical solution. It makes consumer-friendly, low-interest downpayment assistance loans available to qualified California residents for purchasing a newly built home, with no cost to taxpayers.
This is not a handout. Homebuyers must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans.
Prop. 37 is designed for renters, first-time homebuyers, and working families who earn too much to qualify for renter assistance programs, but not enough to save the massive down payment required to buy a home.
“Proposition 37 will boost homeownership without burdening taxpayers. As a state revenue bond, downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers.” -Malia Cohen, California State Controller
BUILDS MORE HOMES, CREATES GOOD JOBS.
California hasn’t built enough homes to keep up with demand. By helping qualified buyers purchase newly built homes, Prop. 37 will help accelerate construction, creating thousands of good-paying jobs and generating economic investment.
Expanding the housing supply helps workers and families to stay in California, build equity, raise their children, and live in the communities where they work.
ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
Taxpayer advocates and California’s Legislative Analyst agree: Proposition 37 has no cost to taxpayers. Loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers-not taxpayers.
STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND CONSUMER PROTECTIONS.
Prop. 37 includes fiscal accountability and transparency requirements, construction accountability standards, and annual audits detailing the status of loans made and the fund’s financial condition.
Consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans, protections from unfair lending practices, strict limits on lender fees, and no penalty for early repayment.
BROAD, BIPARTISAN SUPPORT
Proposition 37 is supported by Democrats & Republicans, labor and businesses, construction workers, taxpayer and housing advocates, veterans, the California Teachers Association, and United Nurses Association of California.
For generations, homeownership provided stability, security, and a path to the middle class. But today, that path is simply out of reach for too many Californians. Proposition 37 is a practical solution that tackles one of the biggest barriers to homeownership, without burdening taxpayers.
Vote YES to expand middle-class homeownership, build more homes, create good jobs, and give working Californians a fair chance to live, work, raise a family, and stay in California.

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers up to 17% of a new home's price:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a chapter to the Health and Safety Code directing CalHFA to run a "Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program" and authorizing it to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, the kind repaid by the program's own income rather than by the state. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm) notes that CalHFA "also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible," and that the measure leaves the rate itself to the agency.
The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. The measure also says these homes are not "public works," so prevailing-wage law does not attach to them by default, and it lets CalHFA write its program rules without going through the Administrative Procedure Act, subject to its own board.
Prop 37's borrower rules set a one-year residency, a 200% of area median income ceiling and a 3% minimum down payment:
Section 51515.01 lists four tests. The applicant must have been "a resident of the State of California for at least one year," must agree to occupy the home as a primary residence within 60 days of closing, must have a family income that "does not exceed 200 percent of the area median income for a family of the same size in the county or metropolitan statistical area where the qualified new home i

CalHFA may add minimum credit scores and debt-to-income limits to satisfy Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or FHA standards, and it may set a longer residency requirement. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0013A1%29.pdf) to the Attorney General makes the point the ballot summary leaves out: an applicant "would not need to be a first-time homebuyer."
The price cap is a formula rather than a dollar figure: 125% of the one-unit conforming loan limit the Federal Housing Finance Agency publishes for the county each year. The FHFA set the 2026 baseline at $832,750 (https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026), up 3.26% from 2025, with a ceiling of $1,249,125 in the highest-cost areas. Applying the measure's formula to the FHFA's county table (https://www.fhfa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-11/FullCountyLoanLimitList2026_HERA-BASED_FINAL_FLAT.xlsx) gives a 2026 cap of $1,040,938 in the 41 counties at the baseline, from Sacramento and Fresno to Riverside and San Bernardino, and $1,561,406 in the ten counties at the ceiling: Los Angeles, Orange, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Santa Cruz and San Benito. Seven counties sit between, including San Diego at $1,380,000 and Ventura at $1,293,750. The income ceiling moves with local incomes in the same way. Using the Department of Housing and Community Development's 2026 State Income Limits (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/income-limits-2026.pdf) as an illustration, a family of four could earn up to $216,200 in Los Angeles County, $261,800 in San Diego County, $401,600 in San Francisco and $194,200 in Fresno or Kern and still qualify. The measure does not say which income table CalHFA must use, so those figures show the shape of the rule rather than the agency's eventual numbers.

Price caps are our calculation from the measure (125% of the county conforming loan limit in the FHFA's annual report). Forty-one counties sit at the 2026 baseline limit of $832,750, so their cap is $1,040,938; ten Bay Area and Southern California counties sit at the $1,249,125 ceiling, so their cap is $1,561,406. Income ceilings use HCD's 2026 State Income Limits as an illustration; the measure says CalHFA will apply "the area median income for a family of the same size in the county or metropolitan statistical area," adjusted for family size, and the agency has not yet said which income table it would use.
PPIC's Eric McGhee calculated (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/) in October that 91% of California renters would have met the income test in 2024, the most recent Census year, and that the price cap "would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024," about 50% above that December's statewide median. Eligibility, he wrote, "is not purchasing power": at 7% mortgage rates and Fannie Mae's 36% debt-to-income ceiling, an entry-level new home was out of reach for 56% of renters even with the down payment solved.
California's existing down payment programs defer repayment while Prop 37's loan is repaid monthly:
CalHFA already runs down payment help, and the comparison explains most of the debate. Its MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) is a "deferred-payment junior loan" of up to 3.5% of the price on an FHA loan or 3% on a conventional one, for first-time buyers within CalHFA's income limits, with nothing due until the home is sold, refinanced or paid off. Its Dream For All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/index.htm) lends up to 20% of the price, capped at $150,000, to first-generation and first-time buyers, and is repaid with the original amount plus 20% of the home's appreciation (15% for buyers at or below 80% of area median income) when the home changes hands. Dream For All is funded by budget appropriations and rationed by lottery; the 2026 application portal closed on March 16 and vouchers went out in May. Proposition 1 on the same ballot would add $1.1 billion (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) in general obligation bond money for homeownership programs of this deferred kind, aimed at low- and moderate-income first-time buyers.
Prop 37's loan is different in three ways. It is open to anyone under 200% of AMI, not only first-time buyers. It is repaid monthly, because the bonds behind it have to be serviced from borrowers' payments. And it is limited to new construction. The California Budget & Policy Center's analysis (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/) puts the first two together: the silent-second structure of today's programs "ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn't compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family's monthly budget," while Prop 37's second mortgage "could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates," because investors in bonds backed by second liens "may therefore require a higher return." The measure's hardship clause lets a borrower ask CalHFA to defer "monthly interest payments" temporarily, which the Budget Center reads as confirmation that monthly payments are the design.
