Builder rules None specific None specific Optional "qualified builder" track: labor standards from the 2025 infill-housing law in exchange for modified construction-defect procedures and a 30% cap on homeowner attorneys' contingency fees
The proponents' case for monthly repayment is the cost it replaces. Buyers who put down less than 20% usually pay private mortgage insurance until they build equity, and the McClatchy editorial board, which recommends (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html) a yes vote, wrote that proponents "have modeled relatively high second-mortgage rates and found buyers could still save money compared with private mortgage insurance." Nothing in the text guarantees a below-market rate; the argument in favor promises "below-market, fixed-rate loans," and the Orange County Register's editorial board wrote (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/) that the claim "rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%," failing which CalHFA "will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates."
Prop 37's qualified builder option trades labor standards for modified construction-defect rules:
Any developer can sell homes into the program. Section 51515.02 adds a voluntary "qualified builder option" for those who certify to CalHFA that their homes will meet the program's eligibility rules; the agency must confirm participation within 30 days, and the letter can be used to market and finance the project. A participating builder takes on the labor and enforcement provisions of Public Resources Code section 21080.66 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=21080.66), the 2025 infill-housing CEQA exemption, which require prevailing wages on fully affordable projects, apply the state's skilled-workforce standards to buildings over 85 feet, extend wage-theft liability under Labor Code section 218.8 to the developer, and let joint labor-management committees sue contractors on workers' behalf. The builder also becomes liable for its contractors' and subcontractors' unemployment-insurance, workers' compensation and licensing violations.
In exchange, homes built under the option get a modified version of the Right to Repair Act's pre-litigation process. A defect notice must identify each home and each alleged violation and be signed by each homeowner; the builder may communicate directly with homeowners during the process; the builder may obtain a written release for completed repairs, which current law, as the LAO's letter notes, does not allow; a builder may move to dismiss a stayed case if the homeowner has not acted within 120 days; and the builder must disclose the special rules in writing before escrow closes. For any qualified new home, built under the option or not, attorneys' contingency fees in a defect case are capped at 30% of the recovery unless a court approves more. The modified procedures fall away if a builder sells a home for more than 25% above the price cap, a point proponent Robert Hertzberg confirmed to the Register's board. The California Conference of Carpenters is a signer of the ballot argument and its affiliates have given $1.7 million to the campaign.
Proposition 37's second mortgages are exempt from a 2025 foreclosure-protection law and carry a 0.5% fee cap:
Section 51515.04 sets the consumer rules. CalHFA must limit lender fees, ban prepayment penalties and require fixed rates. A lender may charge an origination fee of no more than 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater, and no other fee without the agency's approval. An applicant whose credit score falls short may submit bank statements, pay stubs and rent history for "cashflow underwriting." Every applicant must retain a licensed California real estate agent or broker "to ensure that the home buyer receives adequate representation." CalHFA must require homeowner education where it would help and provide for an independent annual audit.
One clause runs the other way. Subdivision (g) states that Civil Code section 2924.13 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2924.13) "shall not apply to any middle-class home ownership loans made under this chapter." That section, added by AB 130 in June 2025, targets dormant second mortgages: it makes it an unlawful practice for a subordinate-mortgage servicer to go three years without writing to the borrower, to skip required transfer notices, or to foreclose on a debt it has reported as written off or after the statute of limitations has run, and it requires a recorded certification of compliance before any nonjudicial foreclosure. Prop 37 loans, which are subordinate mortgages serviced by CalHFA's contracted lenders, would sit outside those rules. The text does not say why.
The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state cost and three unknowns for Proposition 37:
The LAO's ballot analysis and its October 6, 2025 letter reach the same conclusion in nearly the same words: because the measure "uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs." The letter adds that the $25 billion "is in addition to the revenue bonds CalHFA already issues" for its other programs. Both documents then list what cannot be known yet: "the extent to which investors want to buy the bond," "how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options," and "whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying."
The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) does not count Prop 37 at all. It lists two General Fund-supported bonds on this ballot, Propositions 1 and 38, at about $1 billion a year combined, against the roughly $6 billion a year the state already pays on about $80 billion of outstanding bonds. The closest precedent for a self-repaying housing bond is in Prop 1 itself: its $1.25 billion veterans' home-loan bond is repaid by borrowers, and the LAO notes those payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds." The difference is that veterans' bonds are general obligation bonds the state stands behind if payments fall short; Prop 37's are revenue bonds that, by their own terms, it does not. The McClatchy board raised the political version of that risk: borrowers in trouble "will quickly discover that their second mortgage exists because California created and authorized this program," which "could create an expectation that the state bears some responsibility for protecting them."
Proposition 37's reach depends on interest rates and new construction, according to PPIC and the Budget Center:
The campaign says the measure "is expected to spur construction of roughly 190,000 new homes." California YIMBY, which took no position (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-37-2026/), worked the arithmetic the other way: $25 billion over 190,000 homes is about $130,000 of bond money per home, and the group argued "there is no shortage of buyers" for new ownership housing, so the subsidy would mostly raise prices unless it reached weaker markets. PPIC's McGhee estimated that if every loan went to a home at the maximum price with the full 17%, $25 billion would reach about 113,000 buyers; at the full 17% on entry-level homes, about 560,000, which he called "a reasonable central estimate." California would have needed 1.35 million more owner households in 2024 to match the rest of the country, and the 560,000 figure would close about 41% of that gap.
The homeownership gap is the proponents' starting point. The Census Bureau's state table (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates/tab3_state05_2026_hmr.xlsx) puts California's homeownership rate at 54.3% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest of the 50 states except New York (52.4%), against a national rate (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/files/qtr226/Q226press.pdf) of 65.0%. The argument in favor says a 20% down payment on a median home "can require saving over $186,000"; the California Association of Realtors' latest report (https://www.car.org/en/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/august2026sales) put the median existing single-family price at $901,420 in August 2026, which makes 20% about $180,000 and 3% about $27,000. The Budget Center notes that the median California household held "just over $18,000" in checking and savings in 2025, so even 3% "could still almost or entirely clear out" what a typical family has, and that new homes more often carry HOA dues, Mello-Roos assessments and insurance problems in fire-prone areas.
Proposition 37's Yes side reports $30.9 million from Realtors, carpenters and Building a Better California with no opposition committee:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $30.9 million in support of Prop 37 across two committees and no opposition committee large enough to appear. The main committee, "Yes on 37—California Homeownership," lists $23.9 million from its top contributors: $14.85 million from Homeownership for Families, a committee sponsored by the California Association of Realtors whose own top donors are the Realtors' Issues Mobilization PAC and the National Association of Realtors; $6 million from Building a Better California, the committee funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr that is also the main opponent of the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/); $1.25 million from the National Association of Realtors; $1.7 million from three carpenters' union committees; $50,000 from California Forever, the Solano County new-town developer; and $30,358 from the California Democratic Party. The Realtors' Homeownership for Families committee is listed separately with $7 million from the Realtors' PAC and the national association.
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute), which runs through October 6, shows $19.6 million for the Yes committee and "No committees identified" in opposition; the FPPC's later date accounts for the gap. The petition that qualified the measure was paid for by "CA Homes Committee," with major funding from Building a Better California, the California Association of Realtors and the United Brotherhood of Carpenters, according to the Secretary of State's Official Top Funders (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/1990-top-funders-02-02-26.pdf) filing. The Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) lists Robert M. Hertzberg, the former Assembly Speaker and Senate majority leader, as proponent on A.G. File 25-0013A1, titled October 21, 2025. The Budget Center observes that because revenue bonds need no voter approval, the program "could have been enacted legislatively."
The argument for Proposition 37 promises zero taxpayer cost and no argument against was filed:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Danny Curtin of the California Conference of Carpenters, Treasurer Fiona Ma as a CalHFA board member and David West of the California State Commanders Veterans Council, says the measure "creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction—with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS." It says California "has the second-worst homeownership rate in

the nation," that "a traditional 20% down payment can require saving over $186,000," and that the program "is not a handout" because borrowers "must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans." It quotes Controller Malia Cohen: "downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers." The guide's index lists the United Nurses Associations of California, the California Conference of Carpenters and Ma as supporters.
The page for the argument against reads: "NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED." CalMatters' voter guide lists Reform California and the League of Women Voters of California as opponents, summarizing their case as objections to the state entering the mortgage business and to helping buyers only by adding debt. The guide notes that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Proposition 37 leads 61% to 35% with Newsom, Becerra and Democrats in support and editorial boards split:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 61% yes, 35% no and 3% undecided, the strongest support for any of the 14 measures. Democrats back it 76% to 20% and independents 62% to 35%, while Republicans oppose it 62% to 35%. Renters support it 70% to 28% and homeowners 59% to 38%; voters under 35 back it 69% to 26% and those 55 and older 54% to 42%. Five percent named it the measure they are most interested in. UC Berkeley's September poll did not ask about it, and PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.
Governor Newsom endorsed the measure on October 9, saying (https://voteyeson37.com/press-release-governor-newsom-supports-prop-37-to-expand-homeownership-in-california/) in the campaign's release that it is "a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families—at zero cost or risk to taxpayers." Xavier Becerra listed (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/?p=551) it among his yes votes on July 31. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) supports it and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) is neutral, one of two measures on which it takes no side; the other is Proposition 1. The campaign's site lists Controller Cohen, Treasurer Ma, Superintendent Tony Thurmond, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan, Darrell Steinberg, Antonio Villaraigosa, Katie Porter and SEIU among its endorsers.
Editorial boards divided on the second-mortgage question. McClatchy's California papers recommend yes, with stated reservations, on the ground that low-down buyers already pay for private mortgage insurance and that the program "connects assistance to new housing," while asking CalHFA to build a public dashboard of rates, defaults and foreclosures. The San Francisco Chronicle recommends a yes vote, according to CalMatters' roster of editorials. The San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/) recommends no, writing that the measure "doesn't do in the slightest" anything about "shelter's extreme cost," and the Orange County Register recommends no, calling it "a risky $25 billion housing experiment" that leaves income-limited families with "two mortgage payments."
Proposition 37 after November 3 would give CalHFA a year to launch the middle-class homeownership loan:
If Prop 37 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the results, which is due December 11, and CalHFA would have until late 2027 to adopt its rules, sign up lenders and begin selling bonds. The agency would then set the interest rate, the credit standards and the pace of bond sales, which is where the measure's unknowns get answered: whether investors buy second-lien revenue bonds at a rate that undercuts private mortgage insurance, whether builders enroll in the qualified builder option, and whether buyers who can clear 3% and a first mortgage at current rates appear in the numbers the campaign projects. The Legislature could amend the statute only by a 60% vote of each house and only in ways that "further the purposes" of the act. If it fails, CalHFA keeps running MyHome and Dream For All, and the only new homeownership money on this ballot is Proposition 1's $1.1 billion for its deferred-loan programs.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the FHFA's 2026 conforming loan limits and HCD's 2026 income limits, campaign-finance data as of October 14, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party and gubernatorial positions as of October 18, 2026, and polling fielded September 4–10, 2026.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . content.text:
es across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

I'm noting that the latest PPIC poll from October has Prop 37 at 65% yes and 32% no, with majorities across demographic and regional groups. Next I'll look for other recent polls, like UC Berkeley IGS, Emerson, and SurveyUSA, and check for late opposition campaigns and the LA Times endorsement. I also recall that measures above 60% in PPIC's final survey usually pass, and I'm starting to weigh that against bond measures.

Next I'm weighing the historical record: 2020 Prop 13 failed even though bonds usually pass in California. Support for ballot measures can also erode as Election Day approaches. With 65% support and ~$35M behind it, passage looks likely, though I should watch for late anti-tax sentiment or a "vote no on everything" push. I also want to check the Berkeley IGS poll for Prop 37.

I'm noting that an AIMSA poll from Oct 19-24 with 2,000 likely voters puts Prop 37 at 59% support, which makes two polls with it comfortably above 50%. Next I'll check the CalMatters and LA Times voter guides for the opposition case and look for any organized opposition campaign or late spending.

Papers with no endorsement from this set are wrapping up, and newspaper endorsements don't carry much weight anyway. Next I'm looking for endorsements from non-profits, parties, and unions.

I'm going through the endorsement list for Prop 37, marking which groups back it and which don't. CalChamber, California Church IMPACT, Friends Committee on Legislation, SPUR, and the CA Democratic Party are supporting it, while Howard Jarvis and the League of Women Voters are opposed. CPEHN, CalTax, and the CA Republican Party are listed as NP.

I'm weighing the remaining endorsements: the minor parties and the Green Party are opposed, and AFSCME, CFT, the state Labor Federation, and CTA are all in support. Taken together, that points to broad backing from Democrats, labor, and business with no funded opposition, and I'm reasoning from how similar well-polling measures have fared historically.

I'm recalling a few past California propositions to test the poll-versus-outcome pattern. Prop 6 in 2024 failed at roughly 47% yes, with little polling beforehand. Prop 30 in 2022 polled around 41% and lost, while Prop 1 that same year polled near 69% and passed.

I'm checking a list of earlier California bond and initiative measures that failed, including a 2016 revenue bond proposition that would have required voter approval. That makes me think revenue bonds don't normally need a public vote, and that this one reached the ballot only because its proponents chose to put it there.

I'm noting that the ballot label frames the bonds as repaid by mortgage payments rather than the state, with no direct state or local costs. The polling is strong, around 65 to 32, with Republicans nearly split and independents leaning yes, and Democratic turnout enthusiasm in a midterm should help it. The main risk I'm weighing is a late drift toward No as Election Day nears, though the upward trend from 61 to 65 cuts against that.

I'm checking the remaining risks: a late drift toward No, ballot fatigue across the many measures, and whether the "$25 billion" label might prompt reflexive No votes, though PPIC respondents did see that label. I also want to see whether any election results have posted yet, so I'm searching for coverage of Prop 37's outcome.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

I've got Prop 37's support total at about $35 million as of October 30, and no opposition committee has crossed the $1 million reporting line, so the money is lopsided toward Yes. I want to check the Hoover Institution's analysis and any late opposition, and look at how initiatives with no organized opposition have historically performed.

I'm weighing how the state's sour mood might affect Prop 37, since recent bonds like Props 1 and 38 polled lower than it does. I'm also recalling how PPIC's late-October propositions polls compared with actual results, which seem reasonably accurate in direction, though my recall of the exact numbers is shaky.

I'm going back over PPIC's 2022 October survey numbers for the propositions, which were close to the final results for the measures with clear leads. That suggests a 65% Yes on Prop 37 with no organized opposition should hold up. I also want to note that midterm electorates skew older and more homeowner-heavy, though Yes still has majority support among voters 55 and over.

I'm checking whether late worries about the billionaire-tax fight, like the Brin/Doerr money opposing Prop 40, could have spilled over onto Prop 37's Yes side. The main question is whether the Yes campaign got tangled with the No on 40 effort in voters' minds.

I'm checking whether the Brin/Doerr money on the No on 40 side has been tied to messaging around Prop 37 in any way.

I'm checking the 2022 and 2024 California measures next: Prop 30 polled around 41% and failed, Prop 29 failed, and Prop 31 passed. The 2024 Prop 1 behavioral health bond stands out, since PPIC's February poll had it near 63% yes but it only just passed with about 50.2%.

I'm going to check whether PPIC overstated Prop 1 in 2024: if it did by about 13 points, the 65% for Prop 37 would translate to roughly 52%, a closer margin than it looks. I'm also comparing the November 2024 bonds, Prop 4 and Prop 2, where PPIC's October numbers were close to the actual results.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.
More reading
How Prop. 3 fared in Berkeley poll (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-25/la-me-berkeley-poll-september-propositions-billionaires-wealth-tax) (L.A. Times)

Inside the Prop. 3 campaign (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043) (EdSource)
Proposition 4
The basics
Proposition 4 would repeal a 1988 ban on the public funding of campaigns and allow all local and state governments to offer public financing programs with certain conditions.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 4: Allowing public campaign financing in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide)
Prop 4 would repeal California’s 1988 ban on public campaign financing, allowing state and local governments to create programs for candidates seeking office.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Candidates would have to abide by certain expenditure limits and follow strict criteria. Funds could not be used for legal or defense purposes or to repay personal loans, nor could they be pulled from education, transportation or public safety buckets. The ballot measure also prohibits discrimination based on party or whether a candidate is an incumbent or running in opposition.
Dig deeper
Democrats and many good government groups support it. The California Taxpayers Assn. and Reform California oppose it.
Proposition 5
The basics
Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years. In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). But in 2003, Gray Davis was ousted from office (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html) and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger. Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.
Advertisement
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide)
Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
Dig deeper
California’s rules for recalling politicians date to the Progressive era (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html) and were seen at the time as a way to give more power to voters.
But there have been concerns in recent years that the process needs reform, especially after the 2021 recall that Newsom overwhelmingly beat back; it cost local and state governments more than $200 million.
After the Newsom recall failed, the Legislature began a bipartisan task force to suggest changes.
Advertisement
More reading
California’s costly, confusing recall sparks an effort to rethink the rules (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-15/california-costly-confusing-gavin-newsom-recall-rethink-the-rules) (L.A. Times, 2021)
The history of recalls in California (https://www.latimes.com/projects/california-recall-history-insights-from-elections-petitions/) (L.A. Times)
The Little Hoover Commission on recall reform (https://lhc.ca.gov/report/reforming-recall/) (State of California)
Proposition 37
The basics
California’s Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained) would authorize up to $25 billion in down-payment loans for eligible middle-income buyers.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Prop. 37 offers $25 billion to homebuyers to help with a down payment. Here’s the catch (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained)
California’s Prop. 37 could provide $25 billion for homebuyer down payments. Learn how the middle-class housing measure works and its key caveats.
Oct. 24, 2026
The impact
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds. The program would not be funded by taxpayers but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down-payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building. The proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure was approved.
Dig deeper
The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José. Supporters say restricting the program to new homes could spur construction. But critics warn down-payment debt could burden buyers and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.
Proposition 38
The basics
The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year. Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.
Proposition 38 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 38: Immunology and immunotherapy research funding (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide)
Prop 38 aims to fund immunotherapy research to prevent and cure diseases through bonds. An opponent says it is a debt-financed model that prioritizes a few diseases.
Oct. 26, 2026
The impact
The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s. It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.
The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.
Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The Yes on 38 campaign says the proposition pays for itself; 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the state to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. However, it’s difficult to predict whether any research projects will lead to marketable treatments.
Dig deeper
Proposition 38 was backed by organizations including the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research and the ALS Assn. as well as a majority of local chapters of Democratic organizations across the state. Supporters say the proposed funding could give those afflicted with chronic illness hope and potentially more options for treatment.
Its opponents have said the proposed criteria for awarding the grant funding would appear to create an extremely small pool of qualified recipients. Only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, co-founded by billionaire Gary K. Michelson, would qualify under the proposed criteria, according to No on 38.
Advertisement
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for Yes on 38, said “lots of institutions would qualify for funds under this measure.” But she said at a virtual news conference in mid-September that it was “very likely” that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy “will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria.”
Ultimately, Swanson said, the decision lies with the California Department of Public Health.
More reading
An analysis of Prop. 38 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026) (California Legislative Analyst’s Office)
This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) (Cal Matters)
This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) (Cal Matters)
Proposition 39
The basics
Proposition 39 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-39-voting-id-requirements-voter-guide) would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote. In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 39: Stricter voter ID requirements (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-39-voting-id-requirements-voter-guide)
Prop 39 brings the national debate around U.S. election integrity home to California by proposing stricter new voter identification and citizenship verification requirements for state elections.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Opponents contend — as do many independent election experts — that California already has robust measures for verifying the eligibility and identity of voters, and that voter fraud, including by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare. The measure is opposed by the state’s Democratic establishment and prominent civil rights groups, who say it will disenfranchise many eligible voters, particularly those of color, who are poor or live in rural communities. Backers — who include prominent California Republicans and ultrawealthy supporters of President Trump — say it is necessary to prevent voter fraud and block noncitizens from casting ballots. They have provided little evidence of widespread fraud.
Advertisement
Dig deeper
This is part of a larger national campaign. After his return to the White House last year, Trump began a fresh crusade (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing) to rewrite election laws across the country.
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some of California’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they have spent a fortune in an effort to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.
Advertisement
More reading
A powerful union and the birth of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip) (L.A. Times)
Why unions are divided over Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-30/labor-organizers-spearheading-california-billionaire-tax-rebuffed-by-parent-union) (L.A. Times)
The Google co-founder fighting the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax) (L.A. Times)
Inside the massive spending to defeat Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) (L.A. Times)
How the billionaire tax could spark national movement (https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/10/12/the-battle-to-pass-a-billionaire-tax) (The New Yorker)
The academics behind Prop. 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) (Sacramento Bee)
Will Prop. 40 really bring an exodus? (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus) (L.A. Times)
Why healthcare is divided by Prop. 40 (https://www.latimes.com/science/story/2026-09-28/billionaire-tax-is-dividing-california-healthcare-system-its-designed-to-support) (Bloomberg)
Taxing the “ultrarich,” a guide (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/13/magazine/billionaire-wealth-tax-proposition-40.html) (New York Times)
Proposition 41
The basics
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Proposition 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact

content.text:
Yes. Prop 37 will very likely pass. I couldn't find any results yet. The latest pages I found are from November 2, 2026, the day before the election, so this is a forecast and not a result.

- **Polls:** The Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) had it at 65% yes and 32% no in late October, up from 61–35 in September. It was the strongest of the 14 measures on the ballot. A separate AIMSA poll of 2,000 likely voters (October 19–24) found 59% support. PPIC found majorities in favor across regions and demographic groups. Even Republicans were nearly split, 47% yes to 51% no.
- **Money:** The yes side raised about $33–35 million, mostly from the Realtors, the carpenters' unions and Building a Better California. No opposition committee reported any contributions, and no argument against it was filed for the state voter guide.
- **Supporters:** Governor Newsom, Becerra (the Democratic nominee for governor, leading by 24–27 points), the state Democratic Party, the state labor federation, the California Teachers Association, SEIU and the California Chamber of Commerce all back it. The state Republican Party stayed neutral.
- **Opponents:** The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the League of Women Voters, Reform California, a few minor parties and several newspapers oppose it. They ran no paid campaign.
- **Ballot wording:** The ballot summary says "no direct state or local costs," because the homebuyers' loan payments repay the bonds, not taxpayers.

**Caveat:** PPIC has overstated support for bonds before. In the March 2024 primary it had Prop 1 at 59%, and that measure passed with only 50.2%. Even a gap that large would still leave Prop 37 above 50%. In the November 2024 election, PPIC's bond numbers were close to the actual results.
